questions.explanation_text: The electron starts from rest, so its initial velocity is $u=0$ The electric force on the electron is $F=eE$ Using Newton’s second law, $F=ma$ so the acceleration is $a=\frac{eE}{m_{e}}$ Substitute the given values: $a=\frac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(2.0 \times 10^{4})}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}$ $a=\frac{3.2 \times 10^{-15}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}$ $a \approx 3.51 \times 10^{15}\text{m/s}^{2}$ The distance covered is $s=1.5\text{cm}=1.5 \times 10^{-2}\text{m}$ Since the electron starts from rest, $s=\frac{1}{2}at^{2}$ So, $t=\sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}}$ $t=\sqrt{\frac{2(1.5 \times 10^{-2})}{3.51 \times 10^{15}}}$ $t=\sqrt{8.55 \times 10^{-18}}$ $t \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-9}\text{s}$ So the correct option is $2.9 \times 10^{-9}\text{s}$ Option A.

questions.explanation_text: To determine the work done in moving a charge from point B to point A, we use the formula: $\text{W}_{\text{ext}}=q\Delta V$ Where: $q$ is the charge being moved, given as $5\text{mC}$ or $5 \times 10^{-3}\text{C}$ . $\Delta V$ is the change in electric potential between the two points: $V_{f}-V_{i}$ . Given: Potential at point A, $V_{A}=-3\text{V}$ Potential at point B, $V_{B}=5\text{V}$ Substitute these values into the formula: $\text{W}_{\text{ext}}=5 \times 10^{-3}(V_{A}-V_{B})$ $=5 \times 10^{-3}(-3-5)$ $=5 \times 10^{-3} \times (-8)$ $=-40 \times 10^{-3}\text{J}$ $=-0.04\text{J}$ Thus, the work done in carrying the charge from point B to point A is $-0.04\text{J}$ .

To determine the work done in moving a charge from point B to point A, we use the formula:

$\text{W}_{\text{ext}}=q\Delta V$

$q$ is the charge being moved, given as $5\text{mC}$ or $5 \times 10^{-3}\text{C}$ .

questions.explanation_text: Given the problem: Charge $A=+3\text{nC}=3 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$ Charge $B=+1\text{nC}=1 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$ Distance between the two charges: Initial distance, $r_{1}=5\text{cm}=0.05\text{m}=5 \times 10^{-2}\text{m}$ After moving charge $B$ towards $A$ by 1 cm, the new distance is $r_{2}=4\text{cm}=0.04\text{m}=4 \times 10^{-2}\text{m}$ The formula for the work done $(W)$ in moving a charge in an electric field is: $W=U_{B}-U_{A}=\frac{kq_{1}q_{2}}{r_{2}}-\frac{kq_{1}q_{2}}{r_{1}}$ Substituting the values: $\begin{aligned} W & =kq_{1}q_{2}[\frac{1}{r_{2}}-\frac{1}{r_{1}}] \\ & =9 \times 10^{9} \times 3 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^{-9}[\frac{1}{4 \times 10^{-2}}-\frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-2}}] \\ & =9 \times 10^{9} \times 3 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^{-9}[\frac{5-4}{4 \times 5 \times 10^{-2}}] \\ & =27 \times 10^{-9} \times \frac{1}{20 \times 10^{-2}} \\ & =\frac{27}{20} \times 10^{-7} \\ & =1.35 \times 10^{-7}\text{J} \end{aligned}$ Thus, the work done to move charge $B$ towards $A$ by 1 cm is $1.35 \times 10^{-7}\text{J}$ .

Given the problem:

Charge $A=+3\text{nC}=3 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$

Charge $B=+1\text{nC}=1 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$

Initial distance, $r_{1}=5\text{cm}=0.05\text{m}=5 \times 10^{-2}\text{m}$

After moving charge $B$ towards $A$ by 1 cm, the new distance is $r_{2}=4\text{cm}=0.04\text{m}=4 \times 10^{-2}\text{m}$

The formula for the work done $(W)$ in moving a charge in an electric field is:

$W=U_{B}-U_{A}=\frac{kq_{1}q_{2}}{r_{2}}-\frac{kq_{1}q_{2}}{r_{1}}$

Substituting the values:

$\begin{aligned} W & =kq_{1}q_{2}[\frac{1}{r_{2}}-\frac{1}{r_{1}}] \\ & =9 \times 10^{9} \times 3 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^{-9}[\frac{1}{4 \times 10^{-2}}-\frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-2}}] \\ & =9 \times 10^{9} \times 3 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 10^{-9}[\frac{5-4}{4 \times 5 \times 10^{-2}}] \\ & =27 \times 10^{-9} \times \frac{1}{20 \times 10^{-2}} \\ & =\frac{27}{20} \times 10^{-7} \\ & =1.35 \times 10^{-7}\text{J} \end{aligned}$

Thus, the work done to move charge $B$ towards $A$ by 1 cm is $1.35 \times 10^{-7}\text{J}$ .

questions.question_html: $4 \times 10^{10}$ electrons are removed from a neutral metal sphere of diameter 20 cm placed in air. The magnitude of the electric field (in $NC^{-1}$ ) at a distance of 20 cm from its centre is
questions.explanation_text: Given the following parameters: Number of electrons removed $(n)$ : $4 \times 10^{10}$ **Diameter of the sphere $(D):∗∗\text{\(}20\text{cm}$ **Radius of the sphere $(r):∗∗\text{\(}\frac{20}{2}=10\text{cm}=0.1\text{m}$ We need to calculate the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of $20\text{cm}$ from the center of the sphere. The formula for the electric field outside the sphere is: $E=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}r^{2}}=\frac{ne}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}r^{2}}$ Where: $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C}$ (charge of an electron) $\epsilon_{0}=8.854 \times 10^{-12}\text{C}^{2}/\text{N} \cdot \text{m}^{2}$ (permittivity of free space) Since $r=20\text{cm}=0.2\text{m}$ , substituting the values: $E=\frac{4 \times 10^{10} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 9 \times 10^{9}}{(0.2)^{2}}$ Breaking down the calculation: $E=\frac{4 \times 1.6 \times 9 \times 10^{4}}{0.04}=\frac{4 \times 1.6 \times 9 \times 10^{4}}{20 \times 20 \times 10^{-4}}$ Simplifying further: $E=1.6 \times 9 \times 10^{2}=1.44 \times 10^{2}$ Thus, the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of $20\text{cm}$ from the center is: $E=1440\text{NC}^{-1}$

Given the following parameters:

Number of electrons removed $(n)$ : $4 \times 10^{10}$

**Diameter of the sphere $(D):∗∗\text{\(}20\text{cm}$

**Radius of the sphere $(r):∗∗\text{\(}\frac{20}{2}=10\text{cm}=0.1\text{m}$

We need to calculate the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of $20\text{cm}$ from the center of the sphere.

The formula for the electric field outside the sphere is:

$E=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}r^{2}}=\frac{ne}{4\pi\epsilon_{0}r^{2}}$

Where:

$e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{C}$ (charge of an electron)

$\epsilon_{0}=8.854 \times 10^{-12}\text{C}^{2}/\text{N} \cdot \text{m}^{2}$ (permittivity of free space)

Since $r=20\text{cm}=0.2\text{m}$ , substituting the values:

$E=\frac{4 \times 10^{10} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 9 \times 10^{9}}{(0.2)^{2}}$

Breaking down the calculation:

$E=\frac{4 \times 1.6 \times 9 \times 10^{4}}{0.04}=\frac{4 \times 1.6 \times 9 \times 10^{4}}{20 \times 20 \times 10^{-4}}$

Simplifying further:

$E=1.6 \times 9 \times 10^{2}=1.44 \times 10^{2}$

Thus, the magnitude of the electric field at a distance of $20\text{cm}$ from the center is:

$E=1440\text{NC}^{-1}$

questions.question_text: Two spheres of electric charges +2 nC and -8 nC are placed at a distance $d$ apart. If they are allowed to touch each other, what is the new distance between them to get a repulsive force of same magnitude as before?
questions.question_html: Two spheres of electric charges +2 nC and -8 nC are placed at a distance $d$ apart. If they are allowed to touch each other, what is the new distance between them to get a repulsive force of same magnitude as before?
questions.explanation_text: In the initial scenario, two spheres have electric charges $q_{1}=+2\text{nC}=2 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$ and $q_{2}=-8\text{nC}=-8 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$ . The force between them is given by: $F=\frac{k \cdot q_{1} \cdot q_{2}}{d^{2}}$ Substituting the values: $F=\frac{k \cdot (2 \times 10^{-9}) \cdot (-8 \times 10^{-9})}{d^{2}}=\frac{k \cdot (-16 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{2}}$ This is our equation (i). After the spheres are allowed to touch each other, the total charge becomes: $2\text{nC}-8\text{nC}=-6\text{nC}$ Thus, each sphere carries a charge of: $\frac{-6\text{nC}}{2}=-3\text{nC}=-3 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$ The new force $F_{1}$ after separation is: $F_{1}=\frac{k \cdot (3 \times 10^{-9}) \cdot (3 \times 10^{-9})}{d^{'2}}=\frac{k \cdot (9 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{'2}}$ This is equation (ii). To maintain the same magnitude of force as before: $\frac{k \cdot (16 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{2}}=\frac{k \cdot (9 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{'2}}$ Solving for the new distance $d^{'}$ : $\frac{d^{2}}{d^{'2}}=\frac{16 \times 10^{-18}}{9 \times 10^{-18}}=\frac{16}{9}$ Taking the square root: $\frac{d}{d^{'}}=\sqrt{\frac{16}{9}}=\frac{4}{3}$ Therefore: $d=\frac{4}{3}d^{'}$ Solving for $d^{'}$ : $d^{'}=\frac{3}{4}d$ So, the new distance between the spheres to achieve the same magnitude of repulsive force is $\frac{3}{4}d$ .

In the initial scenario, two spheres have electric charges $q_{1}=+2\text{nC}=2 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$ and $q_{2}=-8\text{nC}=-8 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$ . The force between them is given by:

$F=\frac{k \cdot q_{1} \cdot q_{2}}{d^{2}}$

Substituting the values:

$F=\frac{k \cdot (2 \times 10^{-9}) \cdot (-8 \times 10^{-9})}{d^{2}}=\frac{k \cdot (-16 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{2}}$

This is our equation (i).

After the spheres are allowed to touch each other, the total charge becomes:

$2\text{nC}-8\text{nC}=-6\text{nC}$

Thus, each sphere carries a charge of:

$\frac{-6\text{nC}}{2}=-3\text{nC}=-3 \times 10^{-9}\text{C}$

The new force $F_{1}$ after separation is:

$F_{1}=\frac{k \cdot (3 \times 10^{-9}) \cdot (3 \times 10^{-9})}{d^{'2}}=\frac{k \cdot (9 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{'2}}$

This is equation (ii).

To maintain the same magnitude of force as before:

$\frac{k \cdot (16 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{2}}=\frac{k \cdot (9 \times 10^{-18})}{d^{'2}}$

Solving for the new distance $d^{'}$ :

$\frac{d^{2}}{d^{'2}}=\frac{16 \times 10^{-18}}{9 \times 10^{-18}}=\frac{16}{9}$

Taking the square root:

$\frac{d}{d^{'}}=\sqrt{\frac{16}{9}}=\frac{4}{3}$

Therefore:

$d=\frac{4}{3}d^{'}$

Solving for $d^{'}$ :

$d^{'}=\frac{3}{4}d$

So, the new distance between the spheres to achieve the same magnitude of repulsive force is $\frac{3}{4}d$ .
